γράφει· επεχε σεαυτῷ, ἀντὶ τοῦ πρόσεχε σεαυτῷ. Phil 3,8a Εἰ διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ζημίαν

παράθεσιν τῆς ὑπερβολῆς τῶν κρειττόνων ἡγεῖται ζημίαν. 314 Phil 3,8b Τὸ

thought_title: Paul's defenses and gains are proved fruitful by the Philippians; 'as' means intensity; former gains counted loss only by comparison; refuse is part of the stalk
orientation: Oecumenius is explaining Paul's words in Philippians, showing that Paul's defenses, gospel-confirmation, and endurance of bonds are all proved fruitful by the Philippians' faith and steadfastness, then glossing the force of 'as' and the comparison by which former gains are counted loss.
pass_a_gloss: For whether I make my defense when accused because of those who believe, among whom you also are, whether I wish to confirm the gospel to some, it is from your steadfastness; whether I wish to show that I do not endure bonds without profit, it is from your faith. And being found in form as a man. The 'as' is not of likeness but of intensity, as is the saying 'as good is God to Israel,' and 'as I loved your law, Lord,' instead of 'I loved it very much.' Instead of 'holding fast to the word of life.' And to Timothy also he writes: 'pay attention to yourself,' instead of 'attend to yourself.' If he considers it loss because of Christ, they were not bad things; for they were gains. And he said 'I have considered'; for it was not loss, but by comparison with the superiority of the better things he considers it loss. The refuse is part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear of grain once came from the seed.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'steadfastness' for ἔνστασις, the Philippians' firm stand in faith.
Oecumenius contrasts 'as' as expressing intensity, not mere likeness; 'intensity' preserves the rhetorical force.
The passage contrasts former gains with loss by comparison; 'loss' is the standard rendering and matches the argument.
The glossary requires 'refuse' for σκύβαλον, the part of the stalk once useful but now separated.
The glossary requires 'stalk' for καλάμη, representing the law and prophets.
The glossary requires 'ear of grain' for στάχυς, representing Christ.

bible_refs.note: ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας ἐνστάσεως and ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας πίστεως echo Paul's proof from the Philippians' steadfastness and faith.
λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες, glossed as προσέχοντες τῷ λόγῳ τῆς ζωῆς
διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ζημίαν ἡγεῖται and ἥγημαι
ὡς ἀγαθὸς ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ἰσραήλ
ὡς ἠγάπησα τὸν νόμον σου, κύριε

pass_b_english: For whether I make my defense when I am accused for the sake of those who believe, and you are among them, or whether I want to confirm the gospel for some, I do it from your steadfastness. And when I want to show that my chains are not without profit, I prove it from your faith.

Paul says, “And being found in form as a man” (Philippians 2:7). The word “as” does not express likeness but intensity. It is like the phrase “as God is good to Israel” (Psalm 73:1, LXX 72:1), and “as I have loved your law, O Lord” (Psalm 119:97, LXX 118:97), meaning “I have loved it very much.”

When Paul says, “holding fast to the word of life” (Philippians 2:16), he means “paying attention to the word of life.” To Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16), meaning “attend to yourself.”

If Paul considers these things loss for the sake of Christ, they were not bad things; they were gains. And he said “I have considered.” For they were not loss, but by comparison with the surpassing greatness of better things he considers them loss.
The refuse is part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear of grain once came from the seed.
notes: The source contains OCR damage: 'ων' likely represents ὧν, 'οτι' likely represents ὅτι, 'ανθρωπος' likely represents ἄνθρωπος, 'οιόν' likely represents οἷον, 'επεχε' likely represents ἔπεχε, 'ην' likely represents ἦν, 'ηγημαι' likely represents ἥγημαι, 'ειπεν' likely represents εἶπεν, 'ουν' likely represents οὖν, 'ουτως' likely represents οὕτως, 'ηδη' likely represents ἤδη, 'ου' likely represents οὗ, 'αλωνα' likely represents ἅλωνα. The gloss follows the likely readings.

problems.why: This sentence appears with no connection to the surrounding argument about Philippians; reader cannot place it.
problems.fix: Add context: this illustrates that 'as' in Phil 2:7 is idiomatic, like Paul's usage elsewhere.
